segments.text: I don't know how much Sean has told you about... Not very much.
You mentioned that you were...
He was surprised in some cases, but interested in my background.
And said, well, I know somebody who would like to talk to you.
And then...
You mentioned in your email what your phone is.
Yeah.
I'm just, I'd like to do background on people I'm interviewing.
So I did a little digging, and just to see that you worked here in the 90s, is that right?
Did you work here in the 90s?
Is that what the term is?
Yeah, I came 1985, and...
Retired the first one in 2000, then they called me back.
It's like bad cars, they get recalled.
So I retired again in 2002 and again in 2003.
You can't stay away.
Well, my replacement kept either quitting or not coming.
Yeah, I know.
So, and at that time, in fact, that's what I came for, is they had...
the beginning of a separate telecommunication program, separate from electronic, the common base for, I guess, a freshman and sophomore, and then they branch out into a telecom.
And my role was to develop the telecom part.
When they did call me back, I said, well, I'm retired.
They said, yeah.
Okay.
That's a tricky situation.
It's like they got you there.
They know which button to push.
Very much.
I wasn't forced to.
Right.
So I'm going to be honest.
I know
about technology, I'm not very technologically savvy, so I was doing a little background research too into your field, and it very quickly turned into another foreign language to me.
But it was so interesting seeing how you were part of the great technological shift on the university, like you were part of that, you were there, you saw that.
that period of time telecom was booming and the technology was also moving so very fast.
But we actually got after the third year a separate accreditation for the telecom program, EBIT accreditation, so that was good.
Yeah, absolutely.
We were, I think,
The second strictly telecom program, as opposed to electronic, electricity.
and the first undergraduate to get accredited.
So that was good.
Yeah, absolutely.
How was that, sorry that I'm jumping right into this, but how was that process of getting accredited?
Like, what did that entail?
Oh, that's the very long process.
It's a lot, you know, there's this much paperwork.
They want to know all the description of it,
program, how many people, students do you have, how many graduates, how many are employed, etc.
But each course, we get a detail, not just a summary, they want to see everything on the course.
It's a very long preparation process.
And, you know, everybody has to do it, but
Does that go to like, whenever you finish that, does that go to like a national type of?
Yes.
And so you submit that, and so professors of other universities that have a telecom program or something related or are professionally involved in telecom,
review all of these and then decided, yeah, let's go visit or not.
And so there's a group of three or four people that come and spend two or three days here looking at the labs, looking at the talking, interviewing the students.
It's a good process, but it takes a lot of time.
Yeah, I could definitely see that.
I would love to get you in touch with this gentleman named Mark Baggett.
He does the technological services for the library, but he has access to the supercomputers that we have here.
So I was like, I feel like that's something that... Well, that's a different orientation.
Yeah.
Yeah.
But can I rewind and go back a little bit?
Can you tell me about where you were born and where you were raised?
I was born in Paris, France, just before World War II, 1937.
And we had to, because of the German army invasion of France, we had to move
I think three or four times during that period to, well, it's, I was just a kid.
I was a little kid, so, but I do remember suddenly, no, we gotta go.
And it was not like,
Who was in your family at that time?
Well, it's, I was an only child, but my, let's see, yeah, my biological father had to leave because of the war situation.
But later on, I guess, I don't know the details, but my parents divorced.
And again, I know he had gone overseas.
And I don't know the details.
Mother didn't want to talk about it.
But she remarried.
And amazingly, that new father of mine, I mean, he literally adopted me.
And we went through the war.
And he took a chance.
He was, I don't remember which level, co-director of a factory.
And of course, German took that over and so we left again.
So it was, and all the bombardments and this and that.
Can I ask his name and your mom's name?
I don't know if they want that.
Oh, okay, that's fine.
Yeah, I think I'll answer that.
Yeah, absolutely.
Sorry.
No, no, no, that's fine.
Well, actually, my biological father, you can have his first name was Rene, R-E-E.
He had a, from what I read much later on, he had a PhD in marine biology.
Oh, how unique.
And in fact, went to, that was after the war was over, went to New Caledonia, which is a small island in the Pacific, north of New Zealand, way north of it, and set up an aquarium there.
They founded the aquarium and became quite famous in this field.
Wow.
He published three big books.
But I actually only left, that was a year and a half, I think.
And I never met him.
Well, that's on the other side of the world, literally.
Right, yeah.
But your mom, how strong, how strong?
Wow.
Yeah.
She had to face lots of other problems.
Yeah.
Well, the single mother and, you know, the financial input had disappeared, so she had to find a job.
And, yeah, and she has her own Ph.D., Ph.D. in sociology.
Wow.
So I had two...
imposing parents.
Yeah, very educated.
How did you end up in Texas, of all places?
That was a long circuitous study.
I studied in France for high school, of course, and then
junior college, but it was specialized.
It was strictly radio and electronics, except for some civics type.
And then I did my military service in France for three years in their equivalent of the signal corps.
So I was
Since I had done two years of radio school, it made sense for them to put me there.
And after that, I worked in Paris for a year and a half.
And then a friend of mine, who I met in France several times,
said, I had mentioned it.
He said, you know, you need to come and visit us.
And I said, well, yeah, but financialization plus.
He said, well, and then he actually got me a work permit for a year.
So I went there.
And the idea was, well, I'll work and I'll save as much money as possible.
And then I'd play tours.
But it's not the case anymore, but we're talking 1964, 65.
The telecom technology in the US was easily 10 years ahead of the French one.
The telephone network, there was no internet.
digital transmission at that time, but a telephone network in France.
It was not a priority, and the telecom was government-owned, most of Europe.
Oh, I did not know that.
Yeah, almost, yeah, actually all of Europe.
The Postal Service and the telecommunications were government-owned.

And the telephone network, I mean, you know, this is not, it's what, 10 years after the end of World War II, they had a lot of other problems, and their decision was, yeah, we have a telephone network, we'll modernize it later, we gotta use the money.
For other things, yeah.
I discovered that very quickly, that this is fascinating.
I'm a ham radio operator, so I met some American ham.
I was in New Hampshire for that work.
One of them, actually, well,
I told him that my work permit was only expired.
And he said, well, you know, well no.
He had a small repair and installation shop for mobile radios.
And he was specialized in equipping and maintaining radios for fire departments.
Most of them volunteer fire departments around the South New Hampshire.
And he said,
I had the technician who messed up seriously almost six months ago, and I desperately need somebody.
Would you be interested?
Yep.
Well, let's see what I can do.
I guess he convinced the immigration folks that I really need somebody, and I haven't been able to find a small town in New Hampshire.
And so I got another work permit.
That worked out perfectly.
And while I was doing that, I met a young lady who is now my wife, and we've been married for 57 years, I think.
Wow.
So made the right decision, obviously.
So I worked there, and then same thing, you know, one year.
So I went to immigration in Boston and said, is there any way I can renew this?
And I said, no, surely by now I would have been able to find somebody.
Yeah, okay.

And we discussed, and I started the paperwork, and she, I still remember Lizzie went to talk to her boss, I guess, and came back and said, there is one possible, if you can find a teaching job, you can stay, we'll give you a, whatever it's called, it's not the green card, it's
Definitely a work permit and also a temporary status, I guess.
But you can't leave New Hampshire.
I said, okay, I can leave that.
But that was kind of mid-July.
I was like, ooh, school starts in, what, four weeks?
Yeah.
And that was marvelous.
That was the little town in Peterborough, New Hampshire.
Four different families went all around looking for, you know, do you need me?
And I had essentially given up.
I started making reservations to go back.
And I got one of my friend who was the retired Air Force officer, Colonel.
called me and said, I got somebody, but you gotta help.
I said, okay.
Turns out it's a junior college, and their math professor, a lady, turned really sick.
And I said, well, we need somebody to teach you to.
calculus one and two right okay uh i haven't done that but i did study that way back and so
He was the president of the college.
He wrote a letter and said, take that to immigration.
And the same lady said, well, OK, I'm impressed.
So now I had
And that was valid for two years, I think, yeah.
And so, and as I said, I had met my wife there, which, so I have now all kinds of reasons for being nice.
I asked her, it turned out she's from Germany.
which is interesting.
She's much younger than I am.
So we were the start of Europe.
When we decided we got serious with each other, we went to Europe to meet our respective in-laws.
My mother had lots of friends, a lot of friends.
She was working as a translator for German and English to French.
And I knew several of her friends were Jewish and had serious problems during the war.
And here I come with a German girl.
And I thought, well, wait, she's much younger than I am.
That certainly wasn't her fault, but even she was born after the war was over.
So I had all kinds of reasons prepared, but I had forgotten how to
French, especially the Parisians, think.
And they didn't say, but she's German.
They said, wait, she isn't French.
I wasn't prepared for that.
Yeah, well, I didn't go to the U.S. to specifically look for a French girl.
That was funny.
But we got along with our respective in-laws.
So after the two years in the junior college, I decided to go back to school.
So I got a student visa, University of New Hampshire, electrical engineering, and I got bachelor's and master's from there.
And in the process,
somebody say, you know, you're legal with your student status, but you've been here for so long, why don't you try applying for a green card?
And so I did.
And it's when I was a senior at the university,
I got a letter saying, you got the, okay, we've got the green carpet, you gotta go register for the draft.
Oh, the middle of the Vietnam War, right?
So I went there.
And I still remember the master sergeant who was interviewing me.
He said, yeah, OK, so what's your background, et cetera, et cetera.
I said, you know, I just did three years of military.
He said, wrong army buddy.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So sign up here.
And then toward the end, because then I had to take a physical and this, and then I came back to him and he said, you forgot to write your birth date.
Yeah, sorry.
He said, wait, you're over 27.

uh so you're right we need you to register but unless we declare officially a war you know you're too old yeah okay i guess that's accomplished so and uh so i about well several months later i got the green card and oh dang
You get to serve in one army and then almost.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And I wasn't, I had to think about that.
You don't really want to go to Vietnam and fight over there.
Well, yeah, I think it's worth it.
Besides, my wife had no interest in going back to live in Germany.
So she stayed here.
I think I'm staying here.
Yeah.
It's impossible.
What was, did your wife work?
Yeah, she, well, yeah, when I met her, she was working in the pharmacy, not as a pharmacist, but to help the customers and things.
And then when I decided to go to university, she, for some reason, followed me.
And she worked in the pharmacy there, but she was working part-time and going to secretary school.
Wow, okay.
So she was also really busy.
She had a green card already.
Oh, okay.
She came as, you know what au pair?
She was for an American, it was a major, I think.
for whom he babysitted his kids while he was stationed in Germany and done other things.
And so they knew each other very well.
And he said, come on over.
And then she was au pair with them for, I don't know, three years or something like that.
Pretty good amount of time.
Yeah.
so university uh yeah bachelor's master's and then i worked for what was named general telephone which is now uh verizon in in massachusetts just outside of boston
I was with them for five, five years.
And then did something I wanted to do for decades.
I wanted to go overseas and help the people.
But I mean, I'm not, you know, I'm not a doctor and I'm not.
So, but if they need help with,
maybe I can do training and things like that.
And so I had applied to the UN as a specialized agency called the International Telecommunication Union.
And one branch of that is development for less developed countries.
So I applied, I had applied already coming out of the radio school and they said, well, we don't take people at the technician level.
So once I got the actual degree, I reapplied and they said, yeah, that's good.
But we prefer, since you're going in those countries,
you really needed another, I mean, a higher degree.
And it turned out they were absolutely right.
In most of these countries, people will not take, I don't want to call it orders, but directives from somebody who is not at a higher level than they are.
And they were absolutely right.
So, okay, I got my master's and I applied again.
And it's very good.
We'd like to have you, but since you're going to be the specialist over there, they call it an expert, which is unfortunate because then you go there and...
Well, you're expert in everything telecom.
Well, no, I never worked at those guys.
They say they were there.
Anyhow, so you have some experience in the military and some, but again, you need to have a lot of experience, otherwise they're not going to listen to you.
So five years, ooh.
So that's where I went to work for General Telephone.
So after, and while I was there, after the five years, I reapplied.
No, I actually didn't.

We'd like to have you, there are three possible positions for you, and one was Equatorial Guinea,
And, you know, as the name indicates, they're right on the equator, right in Africa.
And so we think temperature and humidity here is bad, but over there, and they don't have air conditioning.
People were telling me, you know, we changed shirts at least twice a day, if not three times.
And I didn't want to go there alone, right?
So by then we had, the twins were born, so no.
Okay, what's the other one?
Saudi Arabia, with my wife and two daughters?
No, sorry.
Well, we have one in Jamaica.
Ah, that sounds good.
So I took that job.
That was for two years.
They asked me to stay for an extra year.

Well, I think I qualified with that.
But Hayden?
Yeah.

You know, they can go around.

They left foreigners alone, which

And people came to ask us,
not for money or, you know, what the heck are you doing here, but are you lost?
Can we help you?
That's different.
So based on that, many other things.
The job was very interesting.
So after discussion with my wife and then three daughters, we went there for three years, which ended up being six.
So did a lot of training and organizations.
And then my next post was going to be, still with the UN, was going to be in Brazil.

I said, you're going to a research center.

Good.

OK, if you say so.

No.

So when are we spending all this time together?
I'd say, yeah, it's a nine-month contract, but you do have 12 months of work, right?

Right.
Admittedly, if I had known ahead of time, I probably wouldn't have taken it.

Yeah, absolutely.
It's, I mean, that...
So, 19 years, 19 and a half years here.
Wow.

that takes a long time.

there.
